meta.name: CWSP-206 Certified Wireless Security Professional
meta.notes: Initial authoring pass. Covers all five CWSP-206 domains: security policy, vulnerabilities/threats/attacks, WLAN security design and architecture, security lifecycle management, and fast/secure roaming. Correct positions distributed A/B/C/D as 2/3/3/2. Option lengths audited so no correct answer is the sole longest in its question.

questions.question: Which WPA3 mechanism prevents an attacker who captures a wireless association from mounting an offline dictionary attack on the passphrase in a personal (PSK-style) deployment?
options: A. WPA2's PBKDF2-derived PSK reused as the direct dictionary root.
B. Simultaneous Authentication of Equals with a Dragonfly key exchange.
C. Opportunistic Wireless Encryption negotiating a per-client PMK on the fly.
D. Fast BSS Transition using the PMK-R0 mobility-domain hierarchy.
questions.explanation: WPA3-Personal replaces the WPA2 4-Way Handshake preauthentication with SAE, a Dragonfly key exchange based on discrete-logarithm cryptography — each passphrase guess forces a fresh live protocol round with the AP, so a captured handshake reveals nothing that lets an attacker try candidates offline. Option A describes WPA2's actual PBKDF2 PSK derivation, which is exactly the weakness SAE was created to remove. OWE encrypts otherwise-open networks but has no passphrase to protect, so it is not the mechanism the question asks about. 802.11r FT accelerates roaming inside a mobility domain and does not defend the user credential.

questions.question: In an 802.1X/EAP-TLS deployment, which cryptographic operation authenticates the RADIUS server to the supplicant during the inner TLS handshake?
options: A. The server presents a shared PSK matching the supplicant's configured passphrase.
B. The supplicant validates the server using a MAC address on the switch access list.
C. The supplicant validates the server certificate chain against a trusted root CA.
D. The server derives the PMK from the supplicant username hashed with SHA-1.
questions.explanation: EAP-TLS is a mutual TLS handshake — the RADIUS server presents an X.509 certificate that the supplicant chains back to a Certificate Authority it has been provisioned to trust; without that trust-anchor validation the client will refuse to send credentials. Option A confuses EAP-TLS with WPA2-Personal, which has no server-side entity at all. Option B misapplies MAC-authentication bypass, an unrelated fallback that authenticates the client's MAC, not the server. Option D describes an invented flow — the PMK is derived after successful EAP authentication from the MSK, never from a hashed username.

questions.question: Which key does the 4-Way Handshake derive between the supplicant and the authenticator to protect the unicast data frames that follow the handshake?
options: A. Group Temporal Key (GTK) used to protect broadcast frames.
B. Pairwise Master Key (PMK) produced by the EAP authentication.
C. Key Encryption Key (KEK) used only to protect key material.
D. Pairwise Transient Key (PTK) covering unicast data frames.
questions.explanation: The 4-Way Handshake mixes the PMK with fresh ANonce and SNonce values plus the two MAC addresses and derives the PTK, which is then split into the Key Confirmation Key (KCK), Key Encryption Key (KEK), and Temporal Key (TK); the TK is the CCMP/GCMP key that protects unicast data frames afterwards. The GTK is delivered inside the same handshake but is the broadcast/multicast key, not the pairwise one the question asks about. The PMK is the input to the handshake, not the per-session output. The KEK is one component of the PTK used only to wrap key material during rekeys, not the encryption key for user data.

questions.question: A WIPS sensor detects an unknown 802.11 access point beaconing a corporate SSID and, on the wired side, observes traffic from that AP's MAC on the internal LAN. How should the WIPS classify this device?
options: A. Rogue AP; contain and trace it to a wired port for removal.
B. Neighbor AP that can be safely ignored as external to the site.
C. Legitimate corporate AP that should be added to the authorized list.
D. Ad-hoc peer using IBSS mode which requires no further follow-up here.
questions.explanation: The WIPS has confirmed both an unknown radio broadcasting a corporate SSID AND the presence of that radio's frames on the internal wired network — together these facts define a rogue AP per CWSP terminology (an unauthorized device attached to the organization's LAN), and correct handling is over-the-air containment plus a wired-side trace to shut the switch port. A neighbor AP is seen on the RF but never appears on the wired side, so it does not match. Auto-adding the device to the authorized list would legitimize an attacker's foothold. Ad-hoc/IBSS mode uses a different frame subtype (no BSSID from an AP) and does not match a beaconing infrastructure BSS.

questions.question: Which specific threat is IEEE 802.11w Protected Management Frames (PMF) designed to mitigate on a WPA2/WPA3 network?
options: A. Offline brute-force attack on captured WPA2-PSK 4-way handshakes.
B. Forged deauth and disassociation frames that disconnect clients.
C. Rogue DHCP servers that misconfigure wireless client IP addresses.
D. Replay of RADIUS Access-Accept messages between the AP and RADIUS server.
questions.explanation: 802.11w defines a set of Robust Management Frames — most importantly Deauthentication and Disassociation — and protects them with a Management MIC IE plus a Broadcast/Multicast Integrity Protocol, so an attacker cannot forge those frames to knock clients off the WLAN. Offline handshake cracking is countered by strong passphrases and WPA3-SAE, not by PMF. Rogue DHCP is a Layer-3 problem that PMF has no visibility into — it operates on 802.11 management frames only. RADIUS transport security is provided by IPsec or RadSec between the AP and RADIUS server, again outside the scope of 802.11w.

questions.question: During an 802.11r Fast BSS Transition inside a mobility domain, which key sits at the top of the FT key hierarchy so a client can roam between APs without re-running full EAP authentication?
options: A. Pairwise Transient Key (PTK) copied verbatim between APs.
B. Group Temporal Key (GTK) distributed by the target AP.
C. Pairwise Master Key R0 (PMK-R0) at the R0 Key Holder.
D. Session-ticket master key that the RADIUS server issues per roam.
questions.explanation: In 802.11r the R0 Key Holder derives PMK-R0 from the MSK produced by the original EAP authentication, then hands per-AP PMK-R1 keys down to each R1 Key Holder (the target APs) inside the mobility domain; a roam is then authenticated with the FT 4-Way Handshake instead of a fresh EAP exchange. Copying a PTK between APs would violate its per-association nonce derivation and is never done. The GTK is a broadcast key and cannot serve as a per-client roaming root. There is no per-roam RADIUS session ticket in the 802.11r flow — RADIUS is touched only at the initial full authentication.

questions.question: Which RADIUS attribute triple is used in an 802.1X Access-Accept response to place a wireless client into a specific 802.1Q VLAN?
options: A. Framed-IP-Address, Framed-Route, Filter-Id, Framed-MTU
B. Called-Station-Id, Calling-Station-Id, NAS-Identifier
C. Service-Type, Class, Session-Timeout, Reply-Message
D. Tunnel-Type, Tunnel-Medium-Type, Tunnel-Private-Group-ID
questions.explanation: RFC 3580 defines dynamic VLAN assignment as Tunnel-Type=VLAN (13), Tunnel-Medium-Type=IEEE-802 (6), and Tunnel-Private-Group-ID set to the VLAN identifier, all returned inside the Access-Accept; the WLAN controller then tags client traffic onto that 802.1Q VLAN. The attributes in option A belong to PPP dial-up profiles and Layer-3 policy, not VLAN steering. The attributes in option B merely identify the AP and client MAC addresses. The attributes in option C annotate policy metadata but do not carry the VLAN identifier that the switch or controller needs.

questions.question: A financial institution mandates that its wireless network use only FIPS 140-2 approved cryptography for data protection. Which 802.11 cipher suite meets that requirement out of the box?
options: A. AES-CCMP (AES-128 in CCM mode) as specified by the RSN.
B. TKIP paired with 802.11's original Michael MIC checksum.
C. WEP using a 104-bit key with IV concatenation on each frame.
D. Plain RC4 with an EAP-derived per-association session key.
questions.explanation: CCMP wraps AES-128 in Counter with CBC-MAC mode; AES has FIPS 197 validation and CCMP itself is a FIPS-approved authenticated-encryption construction, which is why every enterprise WLAN targeting FIPS 140-2 or 140-3 compliance is built on CCMP (or its stronger GCMP-256 sibling at the 192-bit tier). TKIP relies on the Michael MIC and per-packet RC4 keying, and neither is FIPS-approved. WEP was formally deprecated for any regulated environment years ago. Plain RC4 with an EAP-derived key is not part of any FIPS-approved 802.11 cipher suite.

questions.question: Which characteristic distinguishes WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode from standard WPA3-Enterprise?
options: A. It replaces 802.1X with a PSK exchange intended for high-security clients only.
B. It mandates stronger crypto (Suite B / CNSA) for keying and confidentiality.
C. It removes Protected Management Frames as redundant at 192-bit strength.
D. It disables mutual authentication so RADIUS can issue short-lived tickets.
questions.explanation: WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit (the Suite B / CNSA profile) is a coordinated uplift of every cryptographic primitive: AES-GCMP-256 for data confidentiality, HMAC-SHA-384 for key derivation, and elliptic-curve or 3072-bit RSA/DH parameters for authentication credentials — the authentication model stays 802.1X/EAP-TLS. Option A gets it backwards: the 192-bit profile is enterprise (certificate-based) precisely because a PSK cannot supply the required key strength. PMF is not removed but made mandatory at this level. Mutual authentication is retained; there is no ticketing shortcut that skips server or client verification.

questions.question: A café wants to run a public Wi-Fi hotspot that requires no passphrase yet still encrypts each client's traffic against same-SSID eavesdropping. Which mechanism should it deploy?
options: A. Open System authentication behind a captive portal for T&C acceptance.
B. Shared Key authentication using the café's PIN-of-the-day scheme.
C. Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (Wi-Fi Enhanced Open, RFC 8110).
D. WPA2-Personal with the passphrase printed on every receipt.
questions.explanation: OWE (RFC 8110, marketed by the Wi-Fi Alliance as Enhanced Open) performs an unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman exchange as part of association, so each client derives a unique pairwise key and its traffic is encrypted on the RF even though no credential is entered — exactly the 'open but encrypted' property the hotspot needs. Open System with a captive portal only gates the network layer and leaves the RF cleartext, so other patrons still see each other's frames. Shared Key authentication is the deprecated WEP handshake with well-known cryptographic flaws. Publishing a WPA2-Personal passphrase on receipts gives every guest the same PMK, so the pairwise keys are all derivable and provide no privacy against other patrons in practice.
